(CNN) -- Two inmates at New Jersey's Union County Jail made a movie-style escape Saturday and remained at large Monday, according to Union County Prosecutor Ted Romankow. Otis Blunt, left, and Jose Espinosa escaped from the Union County Jail Saturday night, officials say. Twenty-year-old Jose Espinosa and 32-year-old Otis Blunt, who are considered armed and dangerous, were discovered missing from their cells at about 5:15 p.m. Saturday, Romankow said. The men left behind dummies in their beds, cinder block dust and a note wishing authorities "Happy Holidays." Espinosa, who recently pleaded guilty to aggravated manslaughter, was to be sentenced on January 25 and faced a minimum of 17 years in prison. Blunt was being held in lieu of $75,000 bond on weapon and robbery charges. Both men were being housed in the high security area of the multilevel jail, Romankow said. Police said Espinosa and Blunt were in adjacent cells and used a long metal wire to scrape away mortar around the cinder block between their cells and the outer wall in Espinosa's cell. Once the cement block between the cells was removed, they smashed the block and hid the pieces in a footlocker. According to police, Blunt, who is 5 feet 10 inches and weighs 210 pounds, squeezed into Espinosa's cell through an approximately 16- to 18-inch hole. The two inmates wiggled through another 18-inch hole in the outer wall. From a roof landing, the two men "took a running jump or they were standing and they jumped approximately 15 feet out and about 30 feet down," Romankow said. Then they jumped a razor-wire fence onto a New Jersey transit railroad bed to freedom, police said. Authorities found two sets of footprints in the snow heading in opposite directions. At a news conference Monday, Romankow read the note that was found in Espinosa's cell, saying it represented the "arrogance of these two men." "Thank you officer -------- for the tools needed, you're a real pal, Happy Holidays," the note read, with a smiley face drawn next to it. Authorities are investigating the note's claims about the guard, the Associated Press reported. The guard has not turned in a report and disciplinary action has not been taken, Romankow said, according to AP. To delay discovery of the escape, Espinosa and Blunt used dummies made of sheets and pillows in their beds. They also hung photographs of bikini-clad women to hide the holes in the walls, a move reminiscent of a scene in the Hollywood hit "The Shawshank Redemption." Romankow played down the comparison. "I think this is a very serious situation you saw," he said. "I really prefer not to compare with any movie, although I can understand why you might because it does look certainly very similar to some of them. Except in 'The Shawshank Redemption' they had a better poster on the wall." According to police, Blunt tried to escape in September using similar methods. There is an $8,000 reward for the men's capture. Romankow said a statewide hunt is under way, with several agencies involved. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Brian Vitagliano contributed to this report.

They then cleared a razor-wire fence, landing on a New Jersey Transit railroad bed before fleeing. Investigators subsequently found two distinct sets of footprints in the snow heading in opposite directions.

2. They squeezed through the hole in the wall into the utility corridor.
3. They made their way to the roof of the jail.
4. Once on the roof, they used wire cutters (how they obtained them remains a subject of investigation) to cut through a 25-foot chain-link fence topped with razor wire.
5. They jumped from the roof onto the roof of an adjacent two-story county building, slid down a drainage pipe, leaped over another fence, and vanished into the streets of Elizabeth.

---

### The "Thank You" Note

Before leaving his cell, Espinosa left a handwritten note taped to the wall near the hole he had dug. It was addressed to a veteran guard, **Correction Officer Rudolph Ford**. 

The note read:
> *"Officer Ford, happy holidays. You're a good man."* 

It reportedly included a crude drawing of a smiley face or a figure jumping a fence. 

The note was a psychological bomb. Whether it was meant as a genuine compliment to a lenient guard, a taunt to the system, or a deliberate attempt to throw investigators off their track by framing Officer Ford as an accomplice, the impact was devastating.

---

### The Tragic Aftermath for Officer Ford

The escape was not discovered until Saturday afternoon—roughly 18 hours after it happened. The jail was immediately placed on lockdown, and a massive manhunt led by the U.S. Marshals Service was launched.

Systemic failures were instantly exposed. Guards had failed to perform proper headcounts, night checks were missed, and officers were reportedly sleeping or distracted on shift.

Officer Rudolph Ford, a 15-year veteran of the force who was working the floor that night, became the central focus of the internal investigation. Investigators questioned him relentlessly about whether he helped the men or turned a blind eye. 

The pressure proved fatal. On December 17—just two days after the escape—Officer Ford was found dead in his parked car in a local park. He had committed suicide by a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Law enforcement later confirmed that Ford was **not** involved in aiding the escape; he was simply a victim of the escapees' manipulation and the severe shame and stress of the institutional failure.

---

### The Manhunt and Recapture

The escape sparked a nationwide dragnet. However, neither man remained free for long.

* **Jose Espinosa:** He was tracked down first. On January 8, 2008—less than a month after the escape—U.S. Marshals and Mexican authorities apprehended Espinosa in **Puebla, Mexico**, where he was living under an assumed identity.
* **Otis Blunt:** Just a week later, on January 15, 2008, Blunt was located and arrested at a hotel in **El Paso, Texas**, just as he was preparing to cross the border into Mexico.

---

### Consequences and Legacy

The Union County Jail escape resulted in major shakeups:
* **Sentencing:** Both Espinosa and Blunt were returned to New Jersey. Espinosa received an additional 5 years for the escape on top of his manslaughter sentence. Blunt was convicted of robbery and the escape, receiving a long state prison sentence.
* **Jail Reforms:** The escape exposed massive security flaws at the Union County Jail. The warden resigned, several guards faced administrative discipline, and structural improvements (including reinforcing walls and installing better surveillance) were made.

The story remains one of the most famous prison escapes in modern U.S. history—a bizarre mix of pop-culture criminal ingenuity and real-world tragedy.
